A Thousand Years on a Single Page

The thematic study asks one large question: why has the pace and direction of medical change varied across British history? The answer lies in the interaction of seven factors — war, religion and superstition, chance, government, communication, science and technology, and the role of the individual. No single factor dominates the whole sweep. Each rises and falls with the period: religion is decisive in the Middle Ages, science in the late nineteenth century, government in the twentieth. The 16-mark factors essay rewards students who can name the named factor, weigh it against two or three others, and make a clear judgement.

Key Fact

One factor tends to dominate each period. Medieval (c1000–c1500): religion. Early modern (c1500–c1750): the role of the individual. Industrial (c1750–c1900): science and technology. Modern (c1900–today): government. Strong essays explain why the lead factor changes and how the others interact.

Mapping the Seven Factors Across the Sweep

Religion and superstition dominates medieval explanations of disease (divine punishment, saints’ cures, the Black Death of 1348 as God’s anger), preserves classical learning through monastic libraries, and limits dissection until the Renaissance. The role of the individual shapes the early-modern disruption: Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s–90s), Harvey (1628), Sydenham, Hunter, Jenner (1796). Science and technology takes over in the nineteenth century: Pasteur’s germ theory (1860s), Koch (anthrax 1876, TB 1882), Lister’s antiseptic surgery (1867), Snow’s 1854 Broad Street pump, Röntgen’s X-rays (1895). Government dominates the twentieth century: 1875 Public Health Act compulsory, Liberal reforms 1906–11, NHS 1948. War repeatedly accelerates change: Crimean (Nightingale), Boer (Liberal reforms), WWI (transfusion, plastic surgery, X-rays), WWII (penicillin mass production, NHS preconditions). Chance punctuates progress: Paré’s salve, Pasteur’s chicken-cholera culture, Fleming’s mould. Communication spreads everything: the printing press from c1500, the Royal Society from 1660, medical journals like The Lancet, mass-circulation newspapers, the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies.

Structuring the 16-Mark Essay

A top-band essay needs a structure that returns to the named factor in every paragraph, not a tour of all seven. The four-paragraph model works:

Introduction: Define the named factor; state your overall judgement (it was/was not the main factor) in one sentence; flag the two other factors you will weigh. Paragraph 1 — the named factor: Two examples from two periods showing the named factor in action. Paragraph 2 — counter-factor A: Strongest rival factor, with one or two examples, and a sentence explicitly comparing it to the named factor. Paragraph 3 — counter-factor B: Second rival factor, again with comparison back to the named factor. Conclusion: A substantiated overall judgement — not a summary. Say which factor mattered most, in which period, and why.

Worked Example: Was Government the main factor in Improving Public Health?

Government in 1348 was almost absent — the Crown ordered fish carts off the road and prayed. In 1665 it ordered shutting up of plague houses but achieved little. By 1848 the first Public Health Act was adoptive (towns chose to opt in) and largely ignored. The 1875 Public Health Act, after the 1867 working-class franchise and germ theory’s spread, was compulsory and comprehensive. The 1948 NHS was decisive. Across this arc, government strengthens as democracy widens and science explains. Counter-factor: science and technology — without Pasteur (1860s), Koch (1882) and Snow (1854) the 1875 Act would have been a shot in the dark. Counter-factor: the role of the individual — Chadwick (1842 report), Snow, Bevan and Beveridge each translated possibilities into laws. Judgement: government became the main factor only after 1875, and only because science and individuals had given it the tools and the case to act.

Key Fact

Three examples, two periods, one judgement. Strong answers move fluently between periods (e.g. comparing 1348, 1848 and 1948) rather than writing four self-contained mini-essays.

Change, Continuity and Progress

The spec asks not just whether change happened but whether it brought progress. Some change was regression: the loss of Roman aqueducts and bath-houses after c450, replaced by less effective Christian hospitals. Some was sideways: medieval infirmaries served different purposes than classical ones, not necessarily worse. Some was contested: the 1853 Vaccination Act faced organised anti-vaccination resistance, and the 1948 NHS was attacked by the BMA. Strong essays say whose perspective defines progress — what improves life expectancy may not improve patient autonomy; what improves overall health may worsen care for specific groups. The rate of change accelerated unevenly: medieval slow, Renaissance start-stop, nineteenth-century rapid, twentieth-century explosive.

The same mistakes cost marks every year. Do not write in the first person or as a diary entry — that prevents AO2 analytical marks. Do not list factors without weighing them; listing all seven is not analysis. Do not stay in one period — the 16-mark essay requires examples from at least two periods.

Do not give vague figures — ‘a lot of soldiers’ is not 40%; ‘many people’ is not 30.7% of Londoners. Use the named individuals from the spec (Vesalius, Harvey, Paré, Hunter, Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Ehrlich, Simpson, Lister, Snow, Chadwick, Nightingale, Booth, Rowntree, Beveridge, Bevan, Fleming, Florey, Chain) by name and date. Reach a substantiated overall judgement — the conclusion is what separates the top band from the rest.

The Spine of the Course

Across thirteen lessons you have travelled from feudalism to the Equality Act 2010. The seven AQA factors — war, religion, chance, government, communication, the economy, ideas of equality, democracy and representation — together with the role of the individual, are the spine of this thematic study. The 16-mark factors essay is the highest-stakes question on the unit and the place where most students lose marks. The reason is structural: students tell stories rather than weigh causes. This synthesis lesson rebuilds the unit around the factors so you can write to the rubric.

Where Each Factor Matters Most

No factor matters equally across all 850 years. Religion is loudest from 1381 (Ball's preaching) to 1689 (Glorious Revolution), with the 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace and the Civil War as its central case studies. Ideas of representation are central from 1640 to 1832 — Levellers, American Revolution, the Reform Act. The economy and communication dominate from 1832 to the present — Chartism, the Anti-Corn Law League, the General Strike, BLM. War is decisive at specific moments: 1214 (Bouvines), 1642-51 (Civil War), 1914-18 (women's suffrage). Chance is rare but powerful: the Black Death made 1381 possible. Knowing where each factor sits stops you trying to argue, say, that ideas of equality were the main factor in 1381 (they were not — that was economy).

Key Fact

Different factors dominate different eras. Religion runs strongest 1381-1689; ideas of representation 1640-1832; the economy and communication 1832-present. Use this map to choose strong examples for whichever factor the question names — pick examples from the period where the factor was most central.

Reading the Rubric

The 16-mark factors essay is marked against two Assessment Objectives, with 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. AO1 rewards specific historical knowledge — dates, names, events. AO2 rewards explanation and analysis: not just what happened but why it mattered, and how factors interacted. The top band requires substantiated overall judgement on the named factor compared with at least two others. Single-factor or single-period answers cap at the lower bands.

In the exam, before you start writing, spend five minutes building a plan. Step 1: name the factor (the question always asks you to evaluate one). Step 2: list two strong examples that support the named factor as decisive, drawn from at least two of the four parts of the course. Step 3: list two examples that suggest a different factor mattered more. Step 4: choose a defensible judgement — not necessarily ‘agree’ or ‘disagree’, but a calibrated answer such as ‘the named factor was decisive in some periods but secondary in others’. Step 5: choose two contrasting factors to weigh against the named factor, with one example each. The plan turns a 25-minute essay into a structured argument rather than a story.

Worked Example: A Role-of-Individuals Question

Consider a question framed around the role of the individual: have individuals been the main factor in shaping the relationship between citizen and state? A top-band paragraph might run: ‘Individuals like Emmeline Pankhurst gave the women's suffrage campaign visibility and a national leadership; without the WSPU's militancy from 1903 the issue might not have stayed in the news. However, militancy alone did not deliver the 1918 Act — women's war work and the political need to redraw the male franchise mattered as much. The pattern repeats across the course: Wilberforce mattered, but the abolition movement was built by Quakers, freed Africans and a national petitioning campaign. Doreen Lawrence's tenacity forced the Macpherson inquiry, but the Met would not have been deemed institutionally racist without changing public ideas.’

Notice the structure. Each paragraph names the factor, gives a specific example, and then weighs it against another factor. It does not list events. It builds an argument about how factors interact.

Worked Example: A Religion Question

Now take a question on religion as the main factor in causing popular protest. A top-band response would draw examples from at least two parts of the course. From Part 2: the 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace was driven by the dissolution of the monasteries and Catholic identity in the north — 30,000 marched under the Five Wounds of Christ. From Part 1: the 1381 Peasants' Revolt was framed by John Ball's preaching from Genesis. From Part 2: the Civil War was animated by Puritan resistance to Laudian reforms. The weighing comes from showing where religion was the trigger (1536) and where it was the frame for grievances actually rooted in the economy (1381) or ideas (1649). The answer ends with judgement: religion mattered most when other factors were already pressing, providing the legitimating language rather than the underlying cause.

Key Fact

For the top band on a 16-mark factors essay you need a sustained argument addressing the named factor, weighing it against at least two others, with a substantiated overall judgement. The question is set across all four parts of the course, so range as widely as you can: two parts is the working minimum. Single-period answers cap at the lower bands.

Common Pitfalls in Real Scripts

Four problems recur in weak answers. The first is single-period coverage — answers that focus only on, say, the suffragettes without ranging across the course. The second is list-not-judgement: students hand the examiner a sequence of factors without saying which mattered more and why. The third is ignoring the named factor: students write what they know rather than what is asked. The fourth, especially with role-of-individual questions, is treating individuals as causes in isolation, when the specification lists the role of the individual as one factor among many.

The 4 SPaG marks reward consistent accuracy and a wide range of specialist historical terms. Students who avoid historical vocabulary cap themselves at the lower SPaG bands. The vocabulary you should deploy precisely: feudalism, franchise, enfranchisement, parliamentary supremacy, mass movement, direct action, institutional racism. Use them in their proper historical context — ‘franchise extension’ rather than ‘getting the vote’, ‘parliamentary supremacy’ rather than ‘Parliament took over’.

A Final Judgement Framework

The strongest essays end with a clear judgement that does not pretend to a false certainty. Try this structure: ‘Factor X mattered most when [conditions], but factor Y was more important when [other conditions], because [evidence]. Overall, [reasoned conclusion].’ This admits complexity while still committing to an argument. That is what the top band rewards: hold competing factors in mind and still say what you actually think.

The Story of the Course

If you take one larger argument from the course, it is this: the British relationship between citizen and state has changed not by smooth evolution but in waves. Each wave was driven by a particular combination of factors. Magna Carta was government and individual; 1381 was economy and chance; 1536 was religion; 1649 was ideas; 1832 and Chartism were economy and communication; 1918 was war and ideas; 1981 was government and economy. The 850-year arc bends towards a more rights-based citizenship, but never in a straight line and never without organised pressure. That insight, deployed in the conclusion of a factors essay, is what separates the top band from the band below.

A Cathedral as a Statement of Recovery

St Paul’s Cathedral is your specified site for the 2028 exam. The building you can visit is mostly later than 1685, so be clear about what the examiner wants: the Restoration story of the site — the old cathedral’s destruction in the Great Fire of 1666, the argument over what should replace it, Christopher Wren’s designs, and the start of construction in 1675, with the walls rising through the last decade of Charles II’s reign. Read that story and the site becomes a summary of Restoration England: disaster, recovery, the new science, and the alliance of Crown and Church.

Old St Paul's: A Ruin Before the Fire

The medieval cathedral on Ludgate Hill — the highest ground in the City — was one of the largest churches in Europe, and by 1660 one of the shabbiest. Its great spire had been destroyed by lightning in 1561 and never rebuilt; under the Commonwealth the nave had been used as cavalry stables; the fabric was cracked and patched. In August 1666 the young Christopher Wren — an Oxford astronomer turned architect — submitted a report proposing to crown the crumbling crossing with something England had never seen: a dome. Days later, the question became academic.

Key Fact

In the Great Fire of September 1666 (Lesson 6) the cathedral burned with the City around it. Booksellers had stacked their stock in the crypt for safety; it burned with everything else. Falling masonry and melted roof-lead left the great church an unstable shell, and after attempts at patching, demolition was accepted as unavoidable.

Wren and the Battle of the Designs

Rebuilding the cathedral of England’s capital was an argument about what England now was, and it ran for nearly a decade. Wren’s favourite scheme, preserved in the huge oak Great Model of 1673–4, was radical: a centralised church under a vast dome — classical, geometric, continental. The clergy rejected it; a cathedral, they insisted, needed the long nave and choir of English tradition. The compromise came in 1675: the so-called Warrant Design, a conventional long-plan church approved by royal warrant — to which Charles II added a quietly decisive clause, allowing Wren liberty to make ‘variations, rather ornamental than essential’ as the work proceeded. Wren used that licence to transform the approved design, and what rose from 1675 was far closer to his own vision, crowned in the end by the dome the clergy had refused on paper.

Wren was a founder of the Royal Society (Lesson 10) and a professor of astronomy before he was an architect, and his collaborator Robert Hooke — the Society’s great experimenter — helped survey the ruined City and design its rebuilding. St Paul’s is what the new science looked like in stone: structural problems attacked with geometry and experiment. The site ties Lesson 6 (the Fire) to Lesson 10 (the Royal Society) in a single building — a connection worth making.

Paying for It: The Coal Tax

A bankrupt-ish Crown (Lesson 13) could not simply buy a cathedral. The money came instead from the Rebuilding Acts’ coal tax — a duty on every ton of coal landed in London, the fuel of the city’s hearths and trades. It was a shrewd instrument: broad, steady, collected at the port, and paid in pennies by everyone who warmed themselves in the capital. London, in effect, rebuilt its own cathedral by heating itself. The same fund rebuilt dozens of Wren’s parish churches, whose steeples rose around St Paul’s in a single co-ordinated skyline — the most visible public-works programme of the age.

The Building Rises

The foundation stone was laid in June 1675, and by the end of Charles II’s reign in 1685 the choir walls stood well advanced — a working answer, in Portland stone, to anyone who doubted the City would recover. The cathedral took thirty-five years in all: the choir opened for the thanksgiving service for the Peace of Ryswick in December 1697, and Parliament declared the work complete in 1711, with Wren still alive to see it — a cathedral begun and finished under one architect, something no medieval builder ever managed. The dome, rising some 365 feet, made a new crown for London’s skyline on the site where the lightning-struck spire had once stood.

Key Fact

The coal tax under the Rebuilding Acts financed St Paul’s and the rebuilt City churches together — a co-ordinated skyline of Wren steeples around one dome, paid for by a duty on the fuel Londoners burned.

What the Site Shows About Restoration England

Each layer of the story is evidence. The decayed old cathedral shows the scars the Restoration inherited — Reformation, neglect and Civil War abuse written into the fabric. The Fire shows the fragility of the wooden city (Lesson 6). The design battle shows a nation negotiating between tradition and the new — clergy defending the English past, a scientist-architect importing classical Europe, a king umpiring with a clause. The coal tax shows practical, parliamentary finance doing what the royal purse could not. And the rising walls show confidence itself: a regime that had survived plague, fire and the Dutch in three consecutive years (Lessons 5, 6 and 13) declaring in Portland stone that London’s future would outshine its past.

Using the Site in the Exam

Chain features to meanings. Old St Paul’s stabled and spireless → the inheritance of civil war; the crypt of burned books → the Fire’s cost to trade and learning; the Great Model → the ambition of the new science; the clergy’s rejection and the Warrant → the pull of tradition; the ‘ornamental’ clause → how Charles II managed rivals; the coal tax → recovery financed by ordinary Londoners; the walls rising by 1685 → confidence restored within your period. Feature, meaning, link to the statement — and keep your evidence anchored in 1660–1685, using the later completion only as the outcome the period made possible.
